slides: Open by making the hidden-variable shift explicit. The statistical object we can observe is a shadow of a richer complete-data object, so inference must alternate between compatible hidden completions and visible model fitting. The geometry is projection geometry, not a black-box optimizer.

Use the route slide to keep the algorithmic chapter geometric. EM is introduced as alternating projection, then grounded in Gaussian mixture responsibilities, likelihood monotonicity, missing-information diagnostics, data-processing loss, misspecified projection, and an overlap lab that changes the shape of the problem.

The alternating-projection diagram is the conceptual heart. The E-step changes hidden completions while respecting the observed marginal, and the M-step returns to the parametric complete-data model. Each move solves a local problem, which is why the observed likelihood improves without guaranteeing a global optimum.

Responsibilities make hidden labels visible as probabilities. Near a component's center, a point is assigned almost decisively; in the overlap band, the same observation remains compatible with both components. That fuzzy region is not merely uncertainty in a plot; it is missing information.

The likelihood trace is the practical contract of EM. The observed log likelihood rises because the auxiliary function turns a log-of-sum problem into a weighted complete-data problem at the current responsibilities. The surface warns students that local improvement still depends on initialization.

Missing information should be read as a curvature and distinguishability loss. Complete labels would create sharper likelihood curvature, while hidden labels flatten directions that responsibilities can absorb. The information-bar artifact is a compact way to compare what complete data would reveal with what visible data retains.

Coarse graining puts hidden variables into the broader data-processing story. A many-to-one observation map cannot increase KL divergence, so merging states or hiding labels erases distinguishability unless the discarded conditional information is irrelevant for the model being compared.

Misspecification changes the target. If the model family cannot contain the true mixture, estimation aims at the closest available point, not the literal data-generating distribution. The fixed-variance single-Gaussian example makes this projection target visible as the mixture mean.

Use the overlap lab as an active diagnostic. As components move closer or variances grow, responsibilities become less decisive, missing information increases, and the EM path often settles more slowly. The geometry changes because the lifted complete-data families meet at a worse angle.

Close by asking students to identify what each step holds fixed. EM holds the observed marginal fixed during completion and holds the completed empirical distribution fixed during model fitting. That two-step discipline is the durable takeaway for mixture models, coarse observations, and misspecified latent-variable learning.
